transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-07-16
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Rourke (Redwood SE), Priya Das (Redwood SRE Advocate), Carlos Vega (DeepNet PL), Aisha Noor (DeepNet SRE), Tom Becker (DeepNet Security), Mei Lin (DeepNet ML)

Summary:
High-level: deep-dive into DeepNet's private VPC topology and recurring tail-latency spikes when calling Redwood private deployment. Discussed NAT hairpin, PrivateLink routing, DNS resolver TTLs, MTU and fragmentation, KV cache locality, batching tradeoffs and quantization fallbacks. Action items and replay lab planned.

Topics:
- Observed symptomology and traces
- Network topology and egress flow (NAT, PrivateLink, peering)
- DNS and resolver behaviour with split-horizon
- MTU/Hairpinning and TCP retransmits
- KV cache miss amplification and batching implications
- Quantization/throughput tradeoffs for lower-latency SLAs
- Security concerns (mutual TLS, SNI, audit logs)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. I see Carlos, Aisha, Tom, Mei, and our engineers Liam and Priya. We'll try to run through the traces you sent and turn them into concrete next steps. Just quick framing: this is a private VPC deployment, right? Not the hosted API.

[00:18] Carlos: Yes correct, Private deployment in our VPC using PrivateLink - we push requests from our internal services through an egress subnet into the privatelink endpoint Laura spun up. We're seeing intermittent 200-600 ms spikes on what should be p95 around 80-90ms.

[00:35] Liam: Got it. I skimmed the traces pre-meeting. Some spikes line up with DNS lookups and strange 502 timeouts from the egress proxy, others look like KV cache cold misses followed by long first-token generation.

[00:52] Aisha: Quick note, we rotated our NAT gateways last week and we thought that might have helped but the pattern persists, more around weekday night windows.

[01:05] Priya: That is interesting — rotations can change ephemeral port exhaustion patterns or change pathing when you have cross-account privatelink. Also want to confirm MTU — fragmentation can cause jumbo packet issues to surface as retransmits, which can look like latency spikes at the application layer.

[01:20] Tom: From security side, we strictly require mutual TLS and SNI validation on the endpoint side; that added slight overhead but shouldn't be this variable. We are concerned about perf impact if we move to dedicated instances.

[01:35] Liam: Right. Two immediate axes: network-level (DNS, NAT, MTU, hairpinning) and runtime-level (KV cache locality, batching, quantization fallbacks). We'll try to map traces to those. I'll note a few hypotheses then we can dig into logs.

[01:50] Carlos: Cool. Hypotheses?

[01:53] Liam: First: DNS resolver TTLs are causing occasional resolvings to fall back to external resolvers, adding 50-200ms. Second: hairpinning when egressing back to same AZ causes path via NAT + PrivateLink loop, and if connection pools are cold you get TCP handshake penalties. Third: KV cache misses plus synchronous cold-start of model variant (e.g., fallback to a larger precision quant) cause a large first-token latency.

[02:15] Mei: The model variant point — we do sometimes see a fallback to float16 modes because of OOM; could that cause a reload?

[02:21] Priya: Yes, if the runtime detects OOM or degraded quant path it can pull a different kernel or fall back to a different model shard which triggers disk reads and kernel loading. That's typically a multiple-hundred-ms event.

[02:35] Aisha: Our traces show spikes correlated with a small set of user ids, not all traffic. Could be skewed keys and cache thrash.

[02:45] Liam: Exactly. Shard-hot keys cause KV cache amplification when many requests hit cold entries. Batching complicates that: large batch sizes help throughput but increase per-request latency variance when a batch contains requests that need long prep (cold KV, prep quant).

[03:00] Maya: Let's pull up the pcap you shared. Liam did you mark interesting ranges?

[03:06] Liam: Yes — I marked a window around 13:12:40 where p95 jumps to 420ms. In that window you see three things: repeated DNS queries from multiple pods within 400ms, a burst of SYN retransmits, and then a full TLS handshake that takes ~280ms before the application layer gets to token generation.

[03:26] Carlos: So DNS then TLS then token delay, sounds like network preconditions.

[03:29] Priya: Could be resolver chaining + split-horizon. If your VPC resolver forwards to on-prem then to third-party and back, that roundtrip adds up. Also TTLs less than 1s in your app could cause continuous lookups.

[03:44] Tom: We do have a split-horizon resolver for internal hostnames. But the privatelink endpoint is a regional alias that should resolve to a local ENI. Are we sure it's not resolving to public IP sometimes?

[03:56] Liam: The A-records in the pcap show two IPs: one internal ENI and one fallback public IP. During the spikes, calls went to the public IP. That indicates either ephemeral resolution to the public endpoint or the endpoint mapping changed post-NAT rotation.

[04:12] Carlos: Hmm. When we rotated we used a new VPC endpoint in a different account, maybe the endpoint id changed and the resolver cache invalidated causing public fallback.

[04:21] Maya: That matches our earlier note: cross-account privatelink sometimes introduces DNS delay because of cross-region or cross-account aliasing. We have a best-practice checklist we can share.

[04:30] Aisha: Please do. Also any immediate mitigations?

[04:33] Liam: Short term: Pin the endpoint IP(s) in your hosts file for the subset of services that need low p95 — not ideal but can mitigate resolver noise. Also ensure connections reuse TLS session tickets and keepalive so you avoid repeated handshakes. Increase ephemeral port ranges if you see SYN retries due to port scarcity.

[04:50] Priya: We also recommend a pop-up local DNS cache on node (dnsmasq) with explicit TTL controls — that reduces chatter.

[05:00] Mei: On the runtime side what about KV cache — can we pre-warm keys or pin shards to local NVMe?

[05:06] Liam: Yes. Two levers: pre-warm hot prefixes and use sticky routing so the same shard always hits the same server (reduces cold misses). If you use sticky sessions we can recommend a hashing scheme. You can also configure the runtime to keep more of the KV in-resident memory by adjusting cache size / eviction policies.

[05:22] Carlos: We already have an LRU eviction tuned for token length, but we might be thrashing due to very skewed distribution. How do we surface that in Redwood logs?

[05:30] Priya: We'll add KV miss rates per shard to the console and provide a small dashboard. Liam can share a query to extract hot key lists from runtime logs.

[05:40] Liam: I'll add that to action items. Also from the trace there were a few packets showing MSS mismatch — MTU issue — causing fragmentation and retransmits. When MTU mismatches with the privatelink ENI path or if you have intermediate tunnels (on-prem) you can get this.

[05:55] Aisha: We do have IPSEC tunnels for DR between AZs, maybe the DF bit is being dropped or path MTU not discovered properly.

[06:03] Maya: Quick mitigation for MTU: set PMTU discovery on, or set MTU to 1400 on your endpoint ENI to be conservative. Also check for loose or inconsistent TCP MSS clamping in the NAT gateway.

[06:15] Tom: Security question — if we pin IPs or change hosts file, does that break certificate mTLS/SNI semantics?

[06:22] Liam: No, cert verification uses the SAN and SNI; as long as SNI matches and the endpoint serves the correct cert you'll be fine. The bigger issue is pinning might bypass some built-in routing/failover so test failover scenarios.

[06:35] Mei: Back on quantization — we saw occasional falls back to higher-precision kernels. Can that be triggered by transient OOMs during batching?

[06:43] Priya: Yes. If a batch grows larger than the configured footprint and causes memory pressure, the runtime may evict caches or reload kernels at lower speed/precision. That leads to a big spike for that batch. If your request size distribution is skewed it amplifies.

[06:57] Carlos: We do some dynamic batching in our client with deadlines. Might that interact badly with server-side batching?

[07:04] Liam: Combined client+server batching can produce non-linear latencies. For example, client-side micro-batches arriving slightly off schedule can cause the server to assemble a mixed batch with some items needing cache loads leading to tail latency for all items. Setting client-side deadlines a bit lower or enabling priority queues on the runtime can help.

[07:20] Maya: Good call — we can provide server-side priority queues and a config example.

[07:24] Aisha: Also we saw occasional 502s coming from an egress proxy — could that be from header size or SNI mismatch?

[07:31] Liam: 502s often come from a misconfigured egress proxy or if the proxy hits backend capacity limits and returns a 502 early. Check proxy logs for backend timeouts and for body size limits; some proxies default to 1MB and if you're sending big context blobs you might hit that.

[07:49] Carlos: We trim contexts but occasionally send long histories for debugging. We'll check.

[07:55] Priya: One toy test to reproduce: add a synthetic workload that targets one hot key repeatedly and runs through your egress path while we capture packet data. We'll try to reproduce hairpin and a cold KV miss within the same run.

[08:06] Mei: Sounds good. How do we reproduce the quant fallback?

[08:09] Liam: We'll craft a workload that forces large batches and then a sudden spike of very long sequences to create memory pressure. We'll instrument memory and kernel load events in the runtime and capture timestamps.

[08:20] Tom: For auditability we need those logs shipped to our SIEM. Are there out-of-the-box audit log hooks for private deployments?

[08:27] Maya: Yes — Private deployments include audit log connectors (S3/Kinesis/CloudWatch) and a structured audit schema. We'll share the schema and a sample pipeline. Note: shipping frequencies might add small write overhead but not on the request path.

[08:40] Carlos: Good. Back to DNS — you mentioned split-horizon weirdness. How do we force resolution to the ENI?

[08:47] Liam: You can enforce VPC resolver rules: create a resolver rule for the endpoint domain and associate it with your VPC. Also ensure EDNS and DNSSEC options aren't causing fallback. The simplest immediate step: a static hosts entry on the app tier mapping domain to ENI IP (again, short term).

[09:03] Aisha: I'd prefer not to change hosts widely. Is there a recommended TTL?

[09:08] Priya: 60s-300s is typical; for low-latency critical paths we recommend 300s and rely on connection reuse rather than frequent DNS.

[09:18] Maya: Let's spend a few minutes on the KV cache telemetry we can enable quickly. Liam?

[09:22] Liam: We'll enable per-shard metrics: hit_rate, miss_rate, eviction_rate, average_key_ttl, and hot_keys(top 100). We'll also add batch composition metrics: batch_size_distribution, percent_batches_with_cold_load. Those let you see correlation to p95 spikes.

[09:39] Carlos: Can we get alerts when miss_rate > 2% for a shard?

[09:44] Priya: Absolutely, we can add alerts and example thresholds. We'll include playbook steps for remediating: increase shard memory, set sticky routing, or pre-warm keys.

[09:56] Mei: For pre-warm, is there tooling from Redwood to push hot keys?

[10:00] Liam: We have a small CLI tool that replays requests to pre-warm KV entries; we'll share it. It supports concurrency knobs to avoid thrashing.

[10:08] Aisha: Great. Now, a more complex case: what if the NAT gateway is causing hairpin because of asymmetric routing across accounts and ENIs? How do we detect and fix that?

[10:18] Maya: Detect by looking at the source IP in the privatelink logs — if you see your public NAT IP hitting the ENI, that's hairpin. Fix by ensuring the private endpoint is resolvable to the ENI IP and that routing tables prefer local peering paths. Also use cross-account VPC endpoint policies properly so no fallback to public endpoints.

[10:33] Carlos: Do you have a checklist of route table and security group rules to verify?

[10:38] Priya: Yes — we'll add a short checklist: ensure route table entries for egress subnet -> endpoint ENI, verify no 0.0.0.0/0 route that supersedes, check SG outbound rules, validate source/destination check on ENIs, and confirm NAT gateway is not in the primary path for privatelink traffic.

[10:56] Tom: On compliance: we'll need SOC2 artifacts for the private deployment and details on key rotation for KMS.

[11:02] Maya: We'll send SOC2 summary and KMS rotation docs. In private mode you can integrate with your KMS/HSM and control keys; we can show the API.

[11:10] Carlos: Excellent. Anything about batching config we should tune now?

[11:14] Liam: A few knobs: max_batch_size, batch_latency_target (ms), priority queue for short requests vs long sequences, and batch composition threshold (eg don't mix long/short sequences in same batch). Try: reduce max_batch_size by 20% and add a small prioritization for under-512-token requests. That often brings p95 down with small throughput loss.

[11:33] Mei: Quantization: is there a recommended profile for our model size to avoid fallback?

[11:38] Priya: We'll propose a quant profile. For your model (7B-ish), 4-bit quant works but needs kernel support; if your workload has many long sequences prefer 8-bit hybrid to keep memory headroom. We'll send a small matrix mapping sequence length distribution to quant profiles.

[11:55] Carlos: If we adopt a dedicated pool does that remove a bunch of this variability?

[11:59] Maya: Dedicated reduces noisy neighbors but doesn't eliminate network-induced tail. If the variance is network-first (DNS/NAT/hairpin) dedicated helps less. For KV cache cold misses and resource contention dedicated with pinned shards helps a lot.

[12:13] Liam: Also Dedicated gives you capacity isolation so you can bump cache sizes and avoid eviction thrash. It also allows lowering risk of quant fallbacks due to memory pressure.

[12:23] Aisha: Any automated fallback options to reduce user-visible spikes?

[12:26] Liam: Yes — enable async responses with a short initial stub, or use progressive token streaming with immediate partial response. Another pattern: if a request would hit a cold path we can return a lower-fidelity quick answer from a cheaper variant and call higher-precision offline for background enrichment.

[12:42] Tom: That might complicate downstream audit trails, but workable. We'll evaluate.

[12:47] Maya: Ok let's recap and turn into actionable items. We'll also propose a lab slot.

[12:53] Liam: Recap: 1) DNS/Privatelink — configure resolver rules and prefer ENI IPs; 2) MTU/TCP — verify PMTU and set conservative ENI MTU if needed; 3) NAT/hairpin — check route tables and avoid NAT for privatelink traffic; 4) KV cache — enable per-shard telemetry, pre-warm hot keys, sticky routing; 5) Batching/Quant — tune batch sizes and recommend quant profile; 6) Security/compliance — SOC2 artifacts and KMS rotation docs.

[13:20] Carlos: That covers it. For the lab can you run the hairpin reproduction and the KV cache replay?

[13:25] Maya: Yes, we'd like to do a hands-on lab. Carlos, what's your preferred time window?

[13:29] Carlos: Week of 7/25 afternoons PST.

[13:33] Maya: We'll add calendar invites. Liam, Priya — can you own the lab?

[13:36] Liam: Yes, I'll lead the lab, Priya will support.

[13:39] Priya: I'll prepare the telemetry dashboards and alerts.

[13:42] Aisha: We'll prepare a sanitized pcap and some sample workloads to share.

[13:45] Mei: Also Mei will share the model profile and token length distribution.

[13:48] Tom: And we need the SOC2 summary and KMS details before the lab.

[13:51] Maya: We'll send that with the runbook.

[13:54] Liam: One last nit — keep an eye on TLS session cache reuse; some client frameworks create a new TLS socket per request which kills reuse. Use connection pooling.

[14:04] Carlos: We're on node.js right now and some microservices spin up short lived clients. We'll audit that.

[14:09] Priya: If you need a small code snippet we can share for keepalive and agent pooling.

[14:13] Carlos: Please do.

[14:16] Maya: Ok we are at about 43 minutes recorded so far — time check, any other items?

[14:22] Tom: One question on logs: how long can we retain per-token traces for debugging? Storage costs?

[14:28] Maya: You can retain detailed traces for a short retention window (7-30 days) in S3 or your SIEM; we can help size that. For long-term we recommend aggregated metrics and sampling for traces to control cost.

[14:38] Aisha: Sounds good.

[14:40] Mei: Will Redwood provide a sample config for dedicated pool memory tunings?

[14:44] Liam: Yes, we'll provide recommended memory and cache size knobs per model variant.

[14:49] Maya: Ok, last next steps summary which we'll email: topology checklist, SOC2/KMS docs, KV telemetry queries, lab invite for week of 7/25, and the pre-warm CLI and pooling snippet.

[14:59] Carlos: Thanks, appreciate it.

[15:02] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts and action items.

[15:10] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-hearings, some speaker labels approximated, timestamps approximate to show flow.
